(Coastal Living) -- Barefoot on the sandy shore of Catalina Island, Kim Francis shades her eyes from the sun and peers back to mainland California. "I can't believe we're 22 miles from Los Angeles," she says, grinning. "I may never go back." Paddlers can experience Catalina from the water's surface. Behind her, the rugged terrain of Two Harbors stretches over rolling hills crossed by winding paths. Near the ferry dock, the modest village (a gift shop, an activities booth and one restaurant) buzzes with visitors. They come here to Catalina's west end -- away from Avalon, the island's much larger settlement -- to hike and watch wildlife. Many have their first try at snorkeling and paddling, says kayak guide Jason Clarke. Adjusting his colorful mask and snorkel, Jason plunges from the 45-foot catamaran Garibaldi into Isthmus Cove and encourages a tour group to do the same. "You won't find kelp forests like this just anywhere," Clarke says. "And always cross your fingers for a dolphin." Paddlers can experience Catalina from the water's surface, with tours that visit secluded coves and mysterious caves, all open for exploration. A few strokes of the paddle separate kayakers from pelicans, sea lions and a bison, which watches from land. "If his tail wags, the buffalo is in a good mood," says Rod Jackson, who helps run Hummer tours to see bison. "But never get too close." The bison have been on the island since the 1920s, when they were brought in as film extras. Today, they number nearly 250 and are protected by the Catalina Island Conservancy. "Sometimes we get a rebel," Jackson says, gesturing to a lone bison across from the area's only inn, The Banning House Lodge. Free hiking permits allow visitors to wander the island at will. Adrenaline junkies will want to tackle Boushay Trail, which climbs 1,800 feet to Silver Peak, the highest point west of Two Harbors. **(Coastal Living)** — Standing barefoot on Catalina Island’s beach, Kim Francis raises a hand against the glare and looks toward the California mainland. Smiling, she says it is difficult to imagine that Los Angeles is only 22 miles away—and that she may never want to return.

Catalina can be explored at sea level by kayak. Behind Kim, Two Harbors’ rugged landscape unfolds across rounded hills threaded with twisting trails. By the ferry landing, the tiny community—consisting of a gift shop, an activity booth and a single restaurant—is lively with tourists.

Visitors choose Catalina’s western end to escape Avalon, the island’s considerably larger town, and to enjoy hiking and wildlife viewing. According to kayak guide Jason Clarke, many guests also snorkel or paddle for the first time here.

Wearing a bright mask and snorkel, Jason dives from the 45-foot catamaran *Garibaldi* into Isthmus Cove, urging his tour group to follow. He says kelp forests like these are uncommon and adds that everyone should hope for a dolphin sighting.

Guided paddling trips take kayakers to remote coves and intriguing caves that are available to explore. After only a few paddle strokes, visitors may find themselves near pelicans and sea lions—or even within sight of a bison observing from shore.

Rod Jackson, who helps operate Hummer excursions focused on the island’s bison, explains that a wagging tail indicates a contented buffalo. Even so, he warns people never to approach too closely.

Bison have lived on Catalina since the 1920s, when they were imported to serve as movie extras. The herd now includes almost 250 animals, all protected by the Catalina Island Conservancy. Pointing toward a solitary bison opposite The Banning House Lodge—the area’s only inn—Jackson remarks that an occasional animal breaks away from the group.

Visitors may roam the island with free hiking permits. Thrill seekers can attempt the Boushay Trail, which rises 1,800 feet to Silver Peak, the tallest location west of Two Harbors. Hikers who reach the summit are treated to expansive views across the Pacific—and, like Kim Francis, may find themselves reluctant to leave.

### Highlights of the West End

Complete details about every business below are available at **visittwoharbors.com**.

**Stay:** Built in 1910, The Banning House Lodge is a rustic, 11-room bed-and-breakfast without televisions, clocks or telephones. For local camping arrangements, phone **310/510-8368**. Cabin rentals are offered from November through April at **800/626-0720**.

**Play:** Contact the Visitor’s Center at **310/510-4205** or the Dive and Recreation Center at **310/510-4272**. Afishinado Charters provides charter-fishing day excursions to Two Harbors; call **323/447-4669** or go to **fishcatalina.com**.

**Dine:** Fresh seafood dishes, steaks and distinctive mixed drinks are available at the Harbor Reef Restaurant and Harbor Reef Saloon. A recommended specialty is the Two Harbors “Buffalo Milk,” a sweet but potent blend of vodka, liqueurs and whipped cream. Call **310/510-4215**.

Catalina Island’s quieter west end offers a peaceful alternative to the bustling settlement of Avalon. Centered around the small community of Two Harbors, this less-developed part of the island is ideal for visitors seeking solitude, natural beauty, and outdoor adventure.

The surrounding coastline is dotted with secluded coves and caves that can be explored by kayak or paddleboard. Snorkeling excursions and boat tours also provide opportunities to discover Catalina’s clear waters and thriving kelp forests. Along the way, visitors may encounter pelicans, sea lions, and dolphins. Inland, the island is home to nearly 250 protected bison, descendants of animals introduced as film extras during the 1920s.

Those who prefer to explore on foot can obtain a free hiking permit and follow Catalina’s winding trails through its rugged interior. For a more demanding outing, adventurous hikers can tackle the steep Boushay Trail to Silver Peak, where they are rewarded with sweeping views of the Pacific Ocean and the island’s dramatic landscape.

## Discovering Catalina Island’s Wild West End

Just 22 miles off the coast of Los Angeles, Catalina Island feels far removed from the traffic and urban pace of Southern California. While many visitors spend their time in the lively resort town of Avalon, the island’s west end offers a quieter and more rugged experience. Centered around the small village of Two Harbors, this part of Catalina is defined by secluded coves, clear water, rolling hills, and expansive views of the Pacific.

Two Harbors sits on a narrow isthmus between Isthmus Cove and Catalina Harbor. With few buildings and a relaxed waterfront atmosphere, the village makes an ideal base for travelers interested in outdoor recreation. Here, days tend to revolve around the landscape rather than shops or nightlife. Visitors can explore the coastline by kayak, swim through kelp forests, search for wildlife in the island’s interior, or hike to ridgelines overlooking both sides of Catalina.

Kayaking is one of the best ways to experience the west end. Paddlers can follow the rocky shoreline into small bays and coves that are difficult to reach by land. The water is often clear enough to reveal fish and strands of kelp below the surface, while sea lions, harbor seals, and seabirds may appear along the route. Depending on conditions and experience, visitors can take a guided excursion or rent equipment for an independent outing.

Snorkeling provides an even closer look at Catalina’s marine environment. Beneath the surface, tall kelp creates a shifting underwater forest that shelters colorful fish and other sea life. Rocky reefs and protected coves offer opportunities for both beginners and experienced snorkelers, although water temperatures and ocean conditions can change. Wearing a wetsuit and checking local guidance before entering the water can make the experience safer and more comfortable.

The island’s wildlife is not limited to the coast. Guided tours into Catalina’s interior introduce visitors to its rugged terrain and unusual mix of native and introduced species. The Catalina Island fox, found nowhere else in the world, is among the island’s most distinctive residents. Visitors may also spot bald eagles, deer, and the bison that have become an enduring symbol of Catalina. Traveling with a knowledgeable guide offers insight into the island’s ecology, conservation efforts, and human history while reaching areas that may otherwise be difficult to access.

Hiking is another highlight of the Two Harbors area. Trails climb from the village into dry hills covered with coastal scrub, opening onto broad views of the Pacific. From higher elevations, hikers can often see the island’s steep shoreline, neighboring coves, and the narrow strip of land separating the two harbors. Routes range from short scenic walks to demanding sections of the Trans-Catalina Trail, which crosses much of the island’s mountainous interior.

The landscape can be exposed, with limited shade and little water available away from the village. Hikers should carry plenty of drinking water, use sun protection, wear sturdy footwear, and confirm whether permits are required for their planned route. Fog, wind, and heat can all affect conditions, so flexibility is useful when planning a day outdoors.

Despite its remote character, Two Harbors offers the basic services visitors need, including lodging, camping, dining, equipment rentals, and seasonal transportation. Many travelers arrive by ferry, and some visit as part of a sailing trip along the Southern California coast. Because services and schedules may vary by season, reservations and advance planning are recommended.

What makes Catalina’s west end memorable is its balance of accessibility and solitude. It is close enough to Los Angeles for a short getaway, yet quiet enough to feel like a genuine retreat. Whether paddling into a hidden cove, snorkeling beneath a canopy of kelp, watching wildlife in the hills, or standing on a ridge above the ocean, visitors encounter a side of Catalina shaped by nature.

For travelers willing to venture beyond Avalon, Two Harbors reveals an island of open water, wild landscapes, and unhurried adventure—a compelling escape only a short distance from the mainland.

## Coastal Living, Barefoot

Coastal living is a return to what feels natural: open windows, sun-warmed rooms, and the quiet rhythm of waves in the distance. It’s a lifestyle shaped by salt air and soft light, where mornings begin slowly and days are measured by the tides.

Here, barefoot is more than a feeling—it’s a state of mind. It means sandy paths, weathered decks, and the freedom to move effortlessly between home and shore. Interiors are relaxed and inviting, filled with natural textures, ocean-inspired colors, and simple comforts.

Unhurried and uncomplicated, barefoot coastal living celebrates life at its most authentic: close to nature, connected to the moment, and always at ease.
